title: Given two strings, find the length of the shortest string that has both of them as subsequences. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Shortest Common Supersequence (Shortest String Containing Both as Subsequences)

s1_definition.profdef: The Shortest Common Supersequence is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is written only once, and the characters unique to each string are added around it, so the shortest length is the sum of the two lengths minus the longest common subsequence length. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs into one combined log that preserves the order of both, writing the shared events only once. The shortest combined log length is the two lengths added together minus their longest shared ordered overlap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Shortest supersequence length equals the two lengths added minus the longest common subsequence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Shortest Common Supersequence is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is written only once, and the characters unique to each string are added around it, so the shortest length is the sum of the two lengths minus the longest common subsequence length. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs into one combined log that preserves the order of both, writing the shared events only once. The shortest combined log length is the two lengths added together minus their longest shared ordered overlap.

**One line to remember:** Shortest supersequence length equals the two lengths added minus the longest common subsequence.

sections.s2_technical:
A common supersequence must contain both strings as subsequences, which means it must include every character of both while preserving each string's order. The only characters that can be shared between the two strings and written a single time are those in a common subsequence, and to be as short as possible we share the longest common subsequence. Every other character is unique to one string and must appear separately. So the shortest length is the first length plus the second length minus the longest common subsequence length, because that shared part would otherwise be double counted.

We compute the longest common subsequence with the prefix table: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` then return `m + n - dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: for ABAC and BAB the longest common subsequence BA has length two, so the shortest supersequence has length four plus three minus two equals five. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, you can reconstruct the actual supersequence by walking the table and emitting shared characters once, and it is a direct complement of the longest common subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs captured on different nodes into one combined log that preserves the order of events from both, writing any shared event only once to keep the log compact. Naively concatenating duplicates shared events and loses the minimal length. This is exactly how the Shortest Common Supersequence works: it uses the longest common subsequence from the Longest Common Substring pattern to compute the shortest merged length.

The code defines a `LogMergeService` exposing `shortestMergedLength(a, b)` returning the shortest common supersequence length. A `Demo` runs it over two sample log strings and logs the length.

sections.s5_journey:
The inputs are ABAC and BAB. We want the shortest string containing both as subsequences.

Step 1 — We build the longest common subsequence table aligning ABAC down the rows and BAB across the columns.

Step 2 — The B in ABAC matches the B in BAB, and the following A matches an A, so a shared ordered overlap BA builds up to length two.

Step 3 — No longer ordered overlap exists between ABAC and BAB, so the longest common subsequence is two, the pair BA.

Step 4 — The shortest supersequence writes BA once and adds the leftover characters of each string around it, so its length is four plus three minus two.

Step 5 — That gives five, matching a merged log such as ABABC that contains both ABAC and BAB in order. The answer is five. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:33:25 PM com.bank.logmerge.service.LogMergeService shortestMergedLength
INFO: Shortest merged log length = 5
Oct 27, 2026 9:33:25 PM com.bank.logmerge.LogMergeApplication main
INFO: Shortest combined log length is 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: a = "ABAC" (4), b = "BAB" (3)
    │
    ▼
  longest common subsequence table
    │ shared ordered overlap: BA → LCS = 2
    ▼
  shortest supersequence = m + n - lcs = 4 + 3 - 2 = 5
    ▼
  Output: shortest merged length = 5  (e.g. ABABC)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Shortest Common Supersequence is the natural complement of the longest common subsequence, so it lives squarely in the Longest Common Substring pattern. A supersequence has to contain both strings as subsequences, which means it must include every character of both while respecting each string's order. The only characters I can write once and share between the two strings are those that form a common subsequence, and to make the result as short as possible I share the longest common subsequence.

Everything outside that shared subsequence is unique to one string and has to appear on its own, so the shortest length is the first length plus the second length minus the longest common subsequence, because that overlap would otherwise be counted twice. I compute the longest common subsequence with the usual prefix table and apply that formula, which keeps the whole thing in quadratic time and space. I can also reconstruct the actual supersequence by walking the table and emitting each shared character only once.

At the National Bank of India I used this to merge two partial transaction logs captured on different nodes into one compact combined log that preserved the order of both while writing shared events only once. I computed the longest common subsequence and applied the sum-minus-overlap formula. Explaining that the shared subsequence is written once, the unique characters are added around it, and that the length is the two lengths minus the common subsequence is what shows an interviewer I understand this complement within the Longest Common Substring pattern.
